title: Small cellular slices compatible with a prescribed diagram slice
statement:
Work in a fixed universe. Let $\kappa$ be uncountable regular and $\mathcal A$ an ordinary locally $\kappa$-presentable category with small Hom sets. Here locally $\kappa$-presentable means having all small colimits [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] and being generated under small $\kappa$-filtered colimits by a small family of objects whose Hom functors preserve those colimits; regular and $\kappa$-filtered have their union and cocone meanings. Let $D$ be an ordinary category with fewer than $\kappa$ morphisms. Let $f:F\to G$ be a natural transformation of $D$-diagrams in $\mathcal A$. For each $d$, fix a $\kappa$-good $L$-cellular tree with root $F(d)$ and colimit $G(d)$ realizing $f(d)$, with small well-founded indexing poset $T_d$, as in [def-coef-good-cellular-tree]. The attaching arrows of the class $L$ have $\kappa$-presentable endpoints. Write $Y_d(B)$ for its colimit on a downward-closed subset $B\subseteq T_d$, taken in $F(d)/\mathcal A$.

A slice consists of downward-closed subsets $B_d\subseteq T_d$ and maps $Y_d(B_d)\to Y_e(B_e)$ for every arrow $d\to e$ of $D$, making $d\mapsto Y_d(B_d)$ a functor and $F\to Y(B)\to G$ natural transformations whose composite is $f$. An extension of slices means inclusions of their subsets for which the canonical tree-colimit maps form a natural transformation. Given any slice $M$ with subsets $A_d$ (not assumed small in cardinality) and subsets $E_d\subseteq T_d$ with $|E_d|<\kappa$, there exist slices $N,N'$ with subsets $B_d$ and $B_d\cap A_d$, respectively, such that $E_d\subseteq B_d$, $|B_d|<\kappa$, and $N'$ extends to both $N$ and $M$. Thus the canonical maps from the intersection colimits to the two slice colimits are natural. The root and the colimits $F(d),G(d),Y_d(A_d)$ need not be $\kappa$-presentable.

source.place: HTT Lemmas A.3.3.15 and A.3.3.16, printed pp.879-882, specialized to ordinary D (Set enrichment) Read online 2026-10-17; archival HTT WANTED. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Write compositions right to left. For any root $R$, let $\mathcal K_R=R/\mathcal A$. Its Hom sets are small. It has all small colimits: adjoin a new initial indexing vertex with value $R$ and its structural arrows to the underlying diagram; its cocones are exactly cocones under $R$. For a nonempty filtered diagram, the underlying colimit already has this property: the maps from $R$ into its apex agree at common successors. Thus the forgetful functor creates filtered colimits. For $P$ presentable in $\mathcal A$, the free object $\Phi_R(P)=(R\to R\amalg P)$ is presentable in $\mathcal K_R$, since $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal K_R}(\Phi_R(P),Z)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(P,UZ)$. Also $1_R$ is presentable: its Hom functor is singleton, and a nonempty filtered colimit of singleton sets is singleton by the elementwise colimit criterion.

source.place: A.3.3.15 proof, printed p.879: relative compactness in the undercategory; universal-property expansion.

proof.text: Fix $d$ and a downward-closed $B\subseteq T_d$ with $|B|<\kappa$. Regard its restricted tree as a cellular tree in $\mathcal K_{F(d)}$, rooted at $1_{F(d)}$, with attaching endpoints $\Phi_{F(d)}(P_t),\Phi_{F(d)}(Q_t)$. Its cell square is the pushout of $\Phi(P_t)\to\Phi(Q_t)$ along the map to its predecessor object: a map out is exactly a map from that predecessor object and a map from $Q_t$ agreeing on $P_t$. Hence this is precisely the original specified cell square, now under $F(d)$. Colimits under $1_{F(d)}$ are the same as colimits in $\mathcal K_{F(d)}$, since maps out of this initial root are unique. Step 1 gives all colimits, small Hom sets, and presentability of this root and all the free endpoints. Apply [lem-coef-small-tree-presentable-vertices] in this ordinary category, with its small inherited indexing poset $B$. It says that $Y_d(B)$ is $\kappa$-presentable in $\mathcal K_{F(d)}$. This applies also to $B\cap A_d$, and to $B=\varnothing$. It makes no claim about presentability in $\mathcal A$.

source.place: A.3.3.15 proof, printed p.879, compactness sentence, reduced to the existing small-tree theorem by free endpoints.

proof.text: Let $\mathscr P$ be the poset of families $B=(B_d)$ of downward-closed subsets of size less than $\kappa$. It is small, as a subset of the product of the power sets of the small $T_d$. The downward closure of $E_d$ is $\bigcup_{t\in E_d}(\{t\}\cup(T_d)_{<t})$, of size less than $\kappa$ by goodness and regularity. Use it as $B_{0,d}$. Unions of fewer than $\kappa$ members of $\mathscr P$ are again members, so $\mathscr P$ and every tail above a member are $\kappa$-filtered. For every $e$, the diagrams $B\mapsto Y_e(B_e)$ and $B\mapsto Y_e(B_e\cap A_e)$ have colimits $G(e)$ and $M(e)$ on every such tail. Indeed any vertex lies in a small downward closure (inside $A_e$ for the second diagram); union with the tail's lower bound supplies an index in the tail. A cocone family therefore gives a leg at each vertex, independent of choices by taking unions. Every order arrow occurs in one member, so these legs are a cocone on the whole tree, or its restriction to $A_e$. The converse is restriction, giving inverse correspondences of cocones. By Step 1 these presentations also hold in $F(d)/\mathcal A$ after restricting the root maps along any fixed $F(d)\to F(e)$.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16, printed pp.879-882: small downward closures and the filtered presentations used by compactness.

proof.text: Use the preceding presentations in $\mathcal K_{F(d)}$. If $Z$ is one of the small pieces from Step 2, every map from $Z$ to $G(e)$ under $F(d)$ factors through $Y_e(B_e)$ on any specified tail; likewise a map to $M(e)$ factors through $Y_e(B_e\cap A_e)$. This follows by applying presentability to that filtered diagram, then clause (1) of [lem-weil-pbc-filtered-colimit-sets-elementwise]. Two maps from $Z$ to stages of the same presentation which agree in its total colimit become equal at a larger stage by clauses (2)-(3). All these are equalities under the chosen root. Fewer than $\kappa$ factorizations and equality witnesses can be imposed simultaneously by taking a common upper bound in $\mathscr P$. There are fewer than $\kappa$ arrows, objects and composable pairs in $D$: for infinite $|\operatorname{Mor}D|$, its square has the same cardinality by [lem-coef-infinite-cardinal-square-power]; the finite case is immediate.

source.place: A.3.3.15 compactness argument and A.3.3.16 proof conditions (c)-(f), printed pp.879-882; witnesses rather than cancellation.

proof.text:
We construct increasing $B_n\in\mathscr P$. Put $X_n^d=Y_d(B_{n,d})$, $H_n^d=Y_d(B_{n,d}\cap A_d)$, and denote the canonical transitions by $i_n^d:X_n^d\to X_{n+1}^d$, $j_n^d:H_n^d\to H_{n+1}^d$, and $k_n^d:H_n^d\to X_n^d$. Write $g_n^d:X_n^d\to G(d)$ and $m_n^d:H_n^d\to M(d)$ for the canonical maps, and $q^d:M(d)\to G(d)$ for the given slice map. For every $\alpha:d\to e$ choose partial arrows $u_n(\alpha):X_n^d\to X_{n+1}^e$, $v_n(\alpha):H_n^d\to H_{n+1}^e$ under $F(d)$, using $F(\alpha)$ on the target root. Require
$$g_{n+1}^eu_n(\alpha)=G(\alpha)g_n^d,\qquad m_{n+1}^ev_n(\alpha)=M(\alpha)m_n^d,$$
$$k_{n+1}^ev_n(\alpha)=u_n(\alpha)k_n^d.$$
Also require $u_n(1_d)=i_n^d$, $v_n(1_d)=j_n^d$, and, for $n\ge1$,
$$u_n(\alpha)i_{n-1}^d=i_n^eu_{n-1}(\alpha),\qquad v_n(\alpha)j_{n-1}^d=j_n^ev_{n-1}(\alpha).$$
These are partial arrows, not assertions that $B_n$ is already a slice.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16, printed pp.880-882: recursive partial-arrow invariant, including root, identity, transition and intersection equations.

proof.text:
The final invariant, for each composable pair $\alpha:d\to e$, $\beta:e\to h$ and $n\ge1$, is
$$u_n(\beta)u_{n-1}(\alpha)=u_n(\beta\alpha)i_{n-1}^d,\qquad v_n(\beta)v_{n-1}(\alpha)=v_n(\beta\alpha)j_{n-1}^d.$$
Here all maps land at stage $n+1$ in the appropriate target. The starting subsets $B_0$ were chosen in Step 3; there are no arrows at negative stages. To construct stage $n+1$ from $B_n$ and the earlier arrows, apply Step 4 to factor $G(\alpha)g_n^d$ and $M(\alpha)m_n^d$ under $F(d)$, for every arrow $\alpha$. The sources are presentable by Step 2. A common upper member $C\supseteq B_n$ supplies preliminary maps $a_\alpha:X_n^d\to Y_e(C_e)$ and $b_\alpha:H_n^d\to Y_e(C_e\cap A_e)$ with the required global and root equations. The following steps impose the remaining equations by enlargement of $C$.

source.place: A.3.3.15 composition diagrams and A.3.3.16 alternating enlargement, printed pp.880-882; simultaneous partial-map version.

proof.text: First compare $a_\alpha k_n^d$ and the canonical inclusion followed after $b_\alpha$, as maps $H_n^d\to Y_e(C_e)$. Their images in $G(e)$ are equal: the first is $G(\alpha)g_n^dk_n^d$, and the second is $q^eM(\alpha)m_n^d=G(\alpha)q^dm_n^d$, which is the same map since $q^dm_n^d=g_n^dk_n^d$. Step 4 supplies an enlargement where this intersection equation holds. The maps $a_{1_d}$ and the canonical $X_n^d\to Y_d(C_d)$ agree in $G(d)$; the maps $b_{1_d}$ and the canonical $H_n^d\to Y_d(C_d\cap A_d)$ agree in $M(d)$. Use Step 4 to make these identity equations hold as well. At $n=0$ these are all the extra equations. All sources here are small pieces under $F(d)$, hence presentable; no root has been assumed presentable in $\mathcal A$.

source.place: A.3.3.16 condition (f) and A.3.3.15 identity compatibility, printed pp.879-882; explicit global comparison for intersection.

proof.text: For $n\ge1$, compare $a_\alpha i_{n-1}^d$ with the transition out of $X_n^e$ followed after $u_{n-1}(\alpha)$. Their images in $G(e)$ agree by the previously imposed global equation for $u_{n-1}$. For a composable pair $\alpha,\beta$, compare $a_\beta u_{n-1}(\alpha)$ with $a_{\beta\alpha}i_{n-1}^d$. Their images in $G(h)$ are respectively $G(\beta)G(\alpha)g_{n-1}^d$ and $G(\beta\alpha)g_{n-1}^d$, so are equal. The same two comparisons with $b,v,j$ agree in $M(e)$ and $M(h)$ because $M$ is a functor and the previous $v$ arrows have their global equations. Step 4 makes all four types of comparison literal after enlargement: their sources are $X_{n-1}^d$ or $H_{n-1}^d$, presentable under $F(d)$. Choose one upper bound for these witnesses and those of Step 7, postcompose every $a,b$, and call the resulting target family $B_{n+1}$ and maps $u_n,v_n$. Each equation is preserved because enlarging only postcomposes its two sides by the same canonical transition. In particular the equations involving $u_{n-1},v_{n-1}$ have those earlier maps fixed. This completes the induction for every natural number, without cancellation of any tree-colimit map.

source.place: A.3.3.15 two compatibility diagrams and A.3.3.16 conditions (d)-(e), printed pp.880-882; complete equality-witness calculation.

proof.text: Put $B_d=\bigcup_{n<\omega}B_{n,d}$ and $C_d=B_d\cap A_d=\bigcup_{n<\omega}(B_{n,d}\cap A_d)$. They are downward-closed, $E_d\subseteq B_d$, and $|B_d|<\kappa$ since $\kappa$ is uncountable regular. The objects $X^d=Y_d(B_d)$ and $H^d=Y_d(C_d)$ are the colimits of their chains: every vertex and order arrow in each union occurs in one stage, so the cocone argument of Step 3 applies. Let $x_n^d:X_n^d\to X^d$ and $h_n^d:H_n^d\to H^d$ be the canonical legs. The transition equations imply that $x_{n+1}^eu_n(\alpha)$ is a cocone on $(X_n^d)$; hence it defines $U(\alpha):X^d\to X^e$ with $U(\alpha)x_n^d=x_{n+1}^eu_n(\alpha)$. Likewise obtain $V(\alpha):H^d\to H^e$ with $V(\alpha)h_n^d=h_{n+1}^ev_n(\alpha)$.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16 conclusion, printed pp.881-882: countable unions and amalgamation using transition equations.

proof.text:
The identity equations give $U(1_d)x_n^d=x_{n+1}^di_n^d=x_n^d$, so $U(1_d)=1$. For a composable pair, the composition and transition equations give
$$U(\beta)U(\alpha)x_n^d=x_{n+2}^hu_{n+1}(\beta)u_n(\alpha)=x_{n+2}^hu_{n+1}(\beta\alpha)i_n^d=x_{n+1}^hu_n(\beta\alpha)=U(\beta\alpha)x_n^d.$$
Colimit uniqueness gives functoriality. Replacing $U,u,x,i$ by $V,v,h,j$ gives the same proof for $V$. The root equations give natural transformations $F\to X$ and $F\to H$ by their displayed formulas on each stage; every partial map was chosen under $F(d)$. The global equations give natural transformations $X\to G$ and $H\to M$ by checking on $x_n$ and $h_n$. Their composites with the root maps are $f$ and the given $F\to M$, by the tree structure maps. Thus $N=(B,U)$ and $N'=(C,V)$ are slices, with $N'$ mapping naturally to $M$.

source.place: A.3.3.15-16 conclusion, printed pp.881-882: identities, composition, and the maps under F and over G checked on colimit legs.

proof.text:
Let $k^d:H^d\to X^d$ be the canonical map from the intersection colimit. On each leg its naturality square is
$$U(\alpha)k^dh_n^d=x_{n+1}^eu_n(\alpha)k_n^d=x_{n+1}^ek_{n+1}^ev_n(\alpha)=k^eh_{n+1}^ev_n(\alpha)=k^eV(\alpha)h_n^d.$$
Uniqueness for the colimit $H^d$ proves $U(\alpha)k^d=k^eV(\alpha)$. Together with the natural canonical $H\to M$ from Step 10 and the inclusions $C_d\subseteq B_d,A_d$, this proves precisely that $N'$ extends to both $N$ and $M$. The maps $H\to G$ induced through these two routes agree on every leg, so $N'$ is a slice over the original $G$ as required. This includes empty trees, empty intersections and empty $D$; the empty restricted object is its root, and all root equations used above remain valid.

source.place: A.3.3.16 conclusion, printed p.882: explicit naturality of both canonical intersection maps.
